abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by complex biology captured by proteomics, transcriptomics, genetics, and brain imaging. These high-dimensional and correlated data make biomarker discovery challenging. To disentangle biomedical AD data, we propose Conditional Feature Importance (CFI), a theory-grounded framework quantifying the unique contribution of individual or grouped variables in any machine learning model while controlling false discoveries. Across ADNI, BioFINDER, and UK Biobank (nearly 48,000 participants), CFI uncovered a striking contrast between unique versus redundant biomarkers across protein and imaging signatures of AD diagnosis, onset, and progression. Age and neurofilament light chain (NfL) were important for all three outcomes, and A{beta}42 was common to diagnosis and progression. Beyond these shared predictors, in BioFINDER, markers associated with neuronal and synaptic injury, including plasma total tau, CSF -synuclein, and CSF neurogranin, contributed unique predictive information for diagnosis, whereas markers related to the amyloid cascade, CSF p-tau181 and A{beta}40, contributed unique predictive information for progression. APOE {varepsilon}4 offered no unique information once downstream proteins were accounted for, whereas contextual markers such as CSF A{beta}40 emerged only through interactions with other biomarkers. We argue that CFI increases the scientific value of machine learning by providing rigorous statistical insights on complex datasets.
